# The Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking lately about how we're taught to fear incompleteness, yet some of the most beautiful things in life exist in that liminal space—not quite done, not quite begun, suspended in potential.

There's a painting in my mind that I never finished. It was supposed to be a landscape, something with trees and water, but I abandoned it somewhere around the third layer of acrylic. My mother asked why I didn't just complete it, and I realized I couldn't quite explain that finishing it would somehow diminish it. The unfinished painting held infinite possibility. It could become anything. The moment I added that final brushstroke, it would become something specific, something limited, something that could be judged as successful or failed.

This extends to so many things. I think about friendships that fade without explicit endings—you don't have a fight, you just gradually see each other less often, and somehow that feels more honest than many of the friendships that do end with a conversation. There's less pretense in gentle fade-outs. Both people recognize something has shifted without needing to dramatize it.

Or consider conversations that end naturally, mid-thought, when both people understand there's nothing more to say even though the topic isn't technically resolved. Those moments feel richer to me than conversations that are neatly wrapped up with conclusive statements. Reality is rarely conclusive. Our understanding of things remains perpetually incomplete, and I think pretending otherwise is a kind of lie we tell ourselves.

I wonder if this is why I'm drawn to certain books that frustrate other people. The ones where the ending is ambiguous, where character motivations remain somewhat mysterious, where you close the cover and have to sit with uncertainty. Everyone wants to know: Did they end up together? Was the protagonist reliable? What actually happened? But maybe the refusal to answer is the point. Maybe the book is better for it.

This relates to something deeper, I think—the problem with solutions. We're obsessed with them. Every problem needs a solution. Every question needs an answer. Every story needs resolution. But life isn't structured that way. Life is mostly unresolved. Most of our problems don't get solved; they just get slightly better managed, or we adapt to them, or we die with them still unsolved. Most questions don't get answered; we just get tired of asking. Most stories don't have neat endings; they have periods where we stop paying attention.

The grief counselors tell you that you don't "get over" loss; you learn to live with it. That's not completion—that's integration of an unfinished thing into your ongoing life. And somehow that's more honest than the narrative of "closure" that we've convinced ourselves is necessary and possible.

I think about all the projects people abandon. The guitar in the closet, the half-written novel, the course started but not finished, the language app downloaded in January. We treat these as failures, as evidence of our lack of commitment or discipline. But what if they're actually evidence of something else—that we're responsive to what life offers us? That we're willing to try things without needing to be guaranteed we'll finish them?

There's something almost aggressive about the insistence on completion, isn't there? A kind of stubborn assertion of will against the natural entropy and distraction of existence. I admire it sometimes, but I also think it misses something important.

I had a teacher once who said that the difference between a professional and an amateur is that the professional finishes things. She meant well, I think. But I've known professionally finished things that felt soulless, and I've known magnificently unfinished things that felt transcendent. The completion wasn't the difference.

Maybe it's just that the world has enough finished things. Libraries are full of completed sentences. Museums are full of finished paintings. We have thousands of resolved narratives. What we might need more of is the ability to sit with unresolved ones, to find meaning in the incomplete, to understand that a sketch can be more powerful than a detailed rendering, that a suggestion can be more evocative than an explicit statement.

This has practical implications too. I think we're raised to believe that our lives should have a trajectory, a narrative arc, a beginning, middle, and end that makes sense. We should get the job, then move up, then retire happily. We should find the person, fall in love, get married, live ever after. We should discover our passion, pursue it relentlessly, achieve success. But life doesn't work that way. Life is a series of unfinished chapters. New ones start before the old ones end. Sometimes you're living in three different stories simultaneously and they never resolve into one coherent narrative.

And I think if we could make peace with that—if we could stop treating our unfinished lives as failures—we might be happier. We might stop waiting for the moment when everything clicks into place, when we'll finally be ready to be happy, when we'll finally have all the answers. That moment doesn't come. Happiness has to exist in the unfinished spaces, in the questions still being asked, in the projects half-started, in the relationships that are ongoing without clear definition, in the understanding that evolves without ever reaching final form.

The Japanese have a concept, wabi-sabi, that embraces incompleteness and imperfection. There's something wise in that perspective. The cracked tea bowl is more beautiful because of the crack. The garden is more interesting because it's always growing, never finished. The artist is more interesting than the art because the artist is still becoming.

I think I'll keep that painting unfinished. And I'll keep having conversations that trail off. And I'll probably abandon some books before I finish them, and start projects I don't complete, and leave things unsaid that maybe should have been said, and become a person who hasn't figured it all out, probably won't, and is increasingly okay with that.

There's a peace in it, oddly enough. In admitting that you're not going to resolve everything. That some of the best things in life exist in the incompleteness. That becoming is more interesting than being, that potential is more beautiful than manifestation, that an unfinished life honestly lived is better than a perfectly completed life that was never quite real.

And maybe that's a more complete philosophy than I could have articulated if I'd tried to finish it.
